speaker: Casey Handmer
title: Why Elon Outcompetes Everyone | Casey Handmer, Terraform Industries
question: In public institutions, what structural mechanism causes permanent government agencies to become progressively slower and more risk-averse over decades?
guest: The problem of all agencies is that you get a founding team, that team sits in place, they hire people like them, and over time it gets captured and sclerotic and can't do its job anymore. There are four hundred something agencies in the United States, and if they were independently operated businesses with paying customers, they'd be out of business tomorrow. They're funded by the private sector and can never go out of business. In DARPA, if you're an employee you can only be there for a fixed term, and then you're out, so you don't have the problem of people who stay forever. In permanent agencies, anyone who has any degree of risk tolerance or labor market value over time will be attrited from the system because they'll get cross-recruited or leave to do something different. If you solve for the equilibrium, the people who remain are the people who either can't or don't want to leave ever. On average, the character of the organization trends more risk-averse, older, and more conservative in decision-making, so its ability to dynamically execute against its stated goals—and attract new talent—necessarily diminishes.

points.core: Tax-funded agencies lack market bankruptcy pressures that dissolve underperforming organizations.
points.note: Accept: unlike private firms funded by paying customers, tax-funded agencies cannot go out of business, preventing natural organizational life cycles and resource recycling. Do not credit: generic complaints about government waste or bureaucracy.

points.core: Employees with high outside labor-market value steadily exit permanent agencies over time.
points.note: Accept: differential attrition where high-agency, risk-tolerant, or high-market-value staff get recruited away or leave for outside opportunities. Do not credit: generic claims that government pay is lower without the selection-over-time dynamic.

points.core: Long-term equilibrium selects for risk-averse staff who avoid ambitious execution.
points.note: Accept: the remaining population converges toward lifers who cannot or will not leave, shifting decision-making progressively older, more conservative, and less capable of dynamic execution. Do not credit: generic stereotyping of civil servants without the attrition-equilibrium mechanism.

points.core: Growing institutional conservatism progressively undermines the agency's ability to attract dynamic talent.
points.note: Accept: as the organization becomes more sclerotic and risk-averse, recruiting high-caliber new talent becomes increasingly difficult, creating a self-reinforcing decline. Do not credit: generic statements that hiring is hard in government.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core mechanism is asymmetric accountability combined with procedural accretion, a ratchet that turns only one way.

Agencies face lopsided incentives: visible failures (a scandal, a wasted grant, an approved drug that harms people) trigger hearings, audits and career damage, while invisible failures (delays, projects never attempted, benefits forgone) cost officials almost nothing. Each error therefore produces a new rule, review layer or sign-off requirement designed to prevent its recurrence. Because no one is rewarded for removing a safeguard, and whoever does so owns the blame if the problem returns, these rules are almost never repealed. Over decades they accumulate into what is sometimes called "organizational scar tissue" or "sludge."

Several features of permanent agencies reinforce this. Lacking a profit signal or bankruptcy threat, they have no outside force that prunes procedures, so compliance with process becomes the measure of performance (Merton's "goal displacement"). Multiple overseers such as legislatures, courts and inspectors general each add veto points. And as Anthony Downs argued in his life cycle of bureaus, ageing agencies gradually shift from being staffed by zealots to being staffed by "conservers" who prioritize security.

points.why: The response explicitly identifies the absence of a bankruptcy threat as removing an external market discipline on permanent agencies.
quotes: Lacking a profit signal or bankruptcy threat, they have no outside force that prunes procedures

points.why: The response never says that employees with stronger outside opportunities disproportionately leave over time.
The shift toward security-minded staff is asserted without explaining how selective departures leave a more risk-averse workforce.
The response does not connect growing institutional conservatism to a declining ability to recruit dynamic talent.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Permanent government agencies grow slower and more risk-averse primarily through asymmetric accountability coupled with a one-way ratchet of rule accretion. Unlike market firms, permanent public institutions face neither competitive exit nor strong rewards for speed and innovation, whereas visible failures trigger intense legislative, media, and legal punishment. For career officials, the rational strategy is blame avoidance: strictly following procedure shields them from sanction even when outcomes lag, while exercising discretion invites personal risk for minimal upside.

Over decades, this incentive structure drives cumulative procedural sedimentation. Whenever a scandal, mistake, or abuse occurs, lawmakers and agency leaders respond by adding new reviews, sign-offs, and compliance checks to prevent a recurrence. Because repealing an existing safeguard exposes a reformer to severe blame if that specific failure ever happens again, constraints accumulate in only one direction. Without competitive pressure to prune obsolete controls, each layer of rules multiplies internal veto points, narrows operational discretion, and rewards process-oriented personnel over entrepreneurial ones—steadily locking the agency into slower, more defensive decision-making.

points.why: The response explicitly says permanent public institutions are insulated from the competitive exit that can dissolve market firms.
quotes: Unlike market firms, permanent public institutions face neither competitive exit nor strong rewards for speed and innovation

points.why: The response does not describe employees with strong outside options disproportionately leaving over time.
The response attributes defensive decisions to procedural incentives and omits the workforce shift caused by selective departures.
The response does not explain how growing risk aversion makes it progressively harder to recruit dynamic talent.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main mechanism is **procedural accretion driven by asymmetric accountability**.

When something goes wrong, such as fraud, a scandal, a lawsuit or a failed project, the agency, legislators, inspectors general or courts add a rule, review step, sign-off or reporting requirement to prevent it happening again. Those safeguards are almost never removed, because nobody gets blamed for keeping one, while removing one risks blame if the problem comes back. Over decades the layers pile up into what Jennifer Pahlka calls a "cascade of rigidity," Steven Teles calls "kludgeocracy," and Philip Howard and Nicholas Bagley criticize as proceduralism.

Incentives hold the pattern in place. Mistakes an agency makes are visible and punished. The costs of doing nothing, like delays, projects never started or benefits never delivered, are spread out and rarely traced back to anyone. Civil-service protections and permanent tenure reward staff for following procedure rather than for results. Each new rule also builds its own constituency of compliance staff, oversight bodies and interest groups that benefit from it, which echoes Mancur Olson's idea of "institutional sclerosis." Unlike firms, agencies seldom face competition or the risk of shutting down, so the clutter is never cleared out.

points.why: The response explicitly links weak market exit pressures to the persistence of accumulated bureaucracy.
quotes: Unlike firms, agencies seldom face competition or the risk of shutting down, so the clutter is never cleared out.

points.why: The response does not describe employees with stronger outside opportunities leaving at higher rates over time.
The response attributes caution to procedural incentives and omits the selective retention of risk-averse staff.
The response does not link growing institutional conservatism to declining ability to recruit dynamic talent.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Permanent government agencies grow slower and more risk-averse primarily through a one-way ratchet of asymmetric accountability and procedural accretion. Unlike private firms rewarded for successful risk-taking, public officials face stark asymmetry: a successful innovation yields little personal gain, while a single visible failure invites legislative scrutiny, lawsuits, media backlash, and career damage. Whenever an error or scandal occurs, lawmakers, courts, and agency leaders respond by adding new approvals, audits, and compliance rules to prevent a recurrence, yet rarely repeal obsolete ones once a crisis fades. Over decades, these accumulated safeguards multiply internal veto points and shift organizational focus from achieving outcomes to documenting defensible processes. This structure also drives self-selection and cultural ossification—what organizational theorist Anthony Downs called the "law of increasing conservatism." Because advancement depends on avoiding mistakes and mastering complex rules rather than taking initiative, risk-tolerant employees depart while cautious, rule-bound administrators rise to leadership, reinforcing procedural rigidity and slowing the agency further with each passing decade.

points.why: The comparison with private firms concerns rewards for risk-taking and omits the absence of bankruptcy pressure.
The response links risk-tolerant employees’ departures to internal advancement incentives without identifying recruitment or outside opportunities as a driver.
Selective departures and promotions progressively favor cautious leadership and weaken the agency’s ability to act.
quotes: Because advancement depends on avoiding mistakes and mastering complex rules rather than taking initiative, risk-tolerant employees depart while cautious, rule-bound administrators rise to leadership
reinforcing procedural rigidity and slowing the agency further with each passing decade

points.why: The response describes departures and promotions but omits how growing conservatism makes it harder to attract new talent.

models.answer: The mechanism is a ratchet of rules and approvals. After a failure or scandal, oversight bodies add safeguards such as documentation, reviews, and sign-offs. Those safeguards are hard to remove because the official who removes one can be blamed if something goes wrong, while the cost of keeping it is spread across many decisions and is harder to see. Over decades, the layers accumulate. Routine decisions take longer, and officials have stronger incentives to follow precedent or escalate a decision than to exercise discretion.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A common mechanism is the accumulation of rules and approvals. When a visible failure occurs, officials have a strong incentive to add a safeguard. Years later, removing it offers little credit and leaves someone accountable if the failure recurs. A permanent agency can therefore retain old controls even as it adds new ones.

Over decades, each additional review can lengthen the time needed for a decision and give another office a chance to delay it. The same incentives shape individual judgment. Taking an unfamiliar course exposes an official to scrutiny, while following precedent is easier to defend. The costs of waiting are often spread across the public and are harder to trace to any one decision.
